meta.title: Road markings
meta.summary: You will understand which lines you may cross and when, what the yellow markings and transverse markings mean, what the arrows on lanes show, and where markings mean you cannot stop.

lesson.h: What road markings are and what colour they are
p: Horizontal markings are lines, arrows, inscriptions and other signs on the carriageway. They set specific traffic modes and procedures, so their requirements are as binding as the requirements of signs ⟦14⟧.

Markings are white or yellow. Lines 1.4 (no stopping), 1.10 (no parking) and 1.17 (route vehicle stops and taxi ranks) are always yellow. The 1.28 grid, which marks the controlled area of an intersection, is also yellow. Remember: a yellow line at the edge of the road almost always relates to stopping or parking.

Vertical markings (2.1-2.7) are applied to road structures: the piers of bridges and flyovers, bollards on islands, guide posts, barriers and kerbs on hazardous sections. They help you notice an obstruction in time.
lesson.tip: Marking numbers start with 1 for horizontal markings and with 2 for vertical markings.

lesson.h: Solid lines 1.1, 1.2, 1.3: you must not cross
p: Crossing lines 1.1-1.3 is prohibited. There are exceptions for only two of them: you may cross 1.1 and 1.2 to stop on the shoulder, and you may cross 1.1 as an exception when driving around an obstruction, if there is no other way round it. There are no such exceptions for the double solid line 1.3.

On a two-lane road where line 1.1 and (or) sign 3.20 separates the oncoming traffic flows, driving onto the oncoming side is prohibited, except in cases provided for by the Rules ⟦15⟧. On a motorway, in the event of a forced stop, the vehicle is moved to the right of the line marking the edge of the carriageway ⟦16⟧.

A solid line also affects stopping: you must not stop if less than 3 m would remain between your car and the solid marking line (other than the line marking the edge of the carriageway) and this would obstruct traffic ⟦17⟧.
list: 1.1 (solid line) separates oncoming traffic flows and marks lane boundaries in hazardous places, marks the boundaries of carriageway areas where entry is prohibited, the boundaries of parking spaces, and the edge of the carriageway on ordinary roads.
1.2 (wide solid line) marks the edge of the carriageway on motorways.
1.3 (double solid line) separates oncoming traffic flows on roads with four lanes or more.
lesson.tip: You do not cross a double solid line even to turn into a yard or to make a U-turn.

p: Lines 1.5-1.8 may be crossed from either side. But remember: permission to cross a line does not override other rules, for example the prohibitions on overtaking.

On an acceleration lane you build up speed and then change onto the adjacent lane, giving way to those already travelling on the road. Before an exit, change lane onto the deceleration lane in good time and reduce speed only there ⟦18⟧.
list: 1.5 separates oncoming traffic flows on roads with two or three lanes and marks lane boundaries where there are two or more lanes in one direction.
1.6 is the approach line: a broken line whose dashes are roughly 3 times longer than the gaps. It warns that solid line 1.1 or 1.11 will begin shortly.
1.7 (short dashes with equal gaps) marks lanes within an intersection.
1.8 (wide broken line) separates an acceleration or deceleration lane from the main lane.
lesson.tip: If you see during overtaking that the dashes have become long (1.6), finish the manoeuvre and return to your lane.

p: 1.11 consists of a solid line and a broken line side by side. It is applied where changing lane is allowed only from one of the lanes, and also at places for U-turns and for entering or leaving parking areas. You may cross 1.11 from the side of the broken line. From the side of the solid line, only when completing an overtaking manoeuvre or driving around an obstruction.

1.9 marks the boundaries of reversible lanes, where the direction of travel can change, and separates oncoming traffic flows when the lane-control signals are off. If there are no lane-control signals or they are switched off, the line may be crossed when it is to the driver's right. When the lane-control signals are on, it may be crossed from either side if it separates lanes running in the same direction.

When the lane-control signals are switched off, you must immediately change lane to the right, beyond line 1.9. Crossing line 1.9 where it separates oncoming traffic flows is prohibited while the lane-control signals are off. Entering a lane marked on both sides by lines 1.9 is prohibited while the lane-control signal above it is switched off ⟦19⟧.
lesson.tip: At line 1.11, look at the side nearer to you: broken - you may cross; solid - only to return after overtaking or driving around an obstruction.

lesson.h: Transverse markings: where to stop and where to give way
list: 1.12 (stop line) marks the place where a driver stops at sign 2.5 or at a prohibitory traffic light (or traffic controller) signal. Sign 5.33 may be used in its place ⟦20⟧.
1.13 marks a place where, if necessary, you must stop, giving way to traffic on the intersecting road.
1.20 warns that you are approaching marking 1.13.
1.21 (the word “STOP”) warns that you are approaching stop line 1.12, where it is used together with sign 2.5.
lesson.tip: You do not drive over the stop line: the car stops before it, not on top of it.

p: At an uncontrolled crossing, give way to pedestrians who are crossing the carriageway in your direction of travel ⟦21⟧. If a vehicle in the adjacent lane has stopped or slowed down in front of the crossing, you may drive on only after making sure there are no pedestrians in front of it ⟦22⟧.

A pedestrian crossing is marked with signs 5.16.1-5.16.3 and (or) marking 1.14.1-1.14.3 ⟦23⟧: a “zebra crossing” on its own is enough. Stopping on the crossing and less than 5 m before it is prohibited ⟦24⟧, and making a U-turn on it is not allowed either ⟦25⟧.
list: 1.14.1 and 1.14.2 (a “zebra crossing”) mark an uncontrolled pedestrian crossing; the arrows of 1.14.2 show the direction pedestrians walk.
1.14.3 marks a pedestrian crossing where traffic is controlled by traffic lights.
1.15 marks the place where a cycle track crosses the carriageway.

1.18 is lane arrows: they show which directions are allowed at the intersection from that lane. It is used on its own or together with signs 5.8.1, 5.8.2. An arrow allowing a left turn from the far left lane also allows a U-turn from it. An arrow showing a dead end means that turning into the nearest carriageway is prohibited.

1.16.1-1.16.3 mark traffic islands: 1.16.1 where oncoming flows are divided, 1.16.2 where flows in one direction are divided, 1.16.3 where flows merge. Islands, bollards and supports in the middle of the road are passed on the right, unless signs or markings require otherwise ⟦26⟧.
1.19 (warning arrows) indicates that you are approaching a narrowing of the carriageway or lines 1.1 and 1.11.
lesson.tip: If arrow 1.18 shows only ahead, you cannot turn from that lane, even if the intersection is clear.

list: 1.4 (yellow solid line) - stopping is prohibited here. It is applied at the edge of the carriageway or along the top of the kerb, on its own or together with sign 3.27. It does not apply to route vehicles.

1.10 (yellow broken line) - parking is prohibited here, but you may stop. It is used on its own or with signs 3.28-3.30. It does not apply to taxis with the meter running, or to vehicles driven by, or carrying, people with group I or II disability or group III disability with musculoskeletal impairments.
1.17 (yellow zigzag line) - a route vehicle stop or taxi rank. Only category M2 and M3 vehicles may stop at the stopping area and within 15 m of it ⟦27⟧.
1.22 - the road (route) number.

1.23 (the letter “A”) - a lane for route vehicles, other public transport (which includes taxis) and other category M3 vehicles. No one else may drive or stop on it, even where it is separated by a broken line ⟦28⟧. The exception is cyclists and e-scooter riders in the cases set out in para. 166 and 168-1.
1.28 (yellow grid) - the controlled area of an intersection. If there is a traffic jam beyond the intersection, you must not enter it ⟦29⟧.

lesson.h: When markings and other signals disagree
list: You must follow the traffic controller's signals, even if they conflict with traffic lights, signs or markings ⟦30⟧.
If the meanings of signs, including temporary ones, and marking lines conflict with each other, or the markings are hard to see (for example, under snow), you are guided by the signs ⟦31⟧.

At road works and places with a temporary change to traffic, temporary signs on a yellow background are put up ⟦32⟧. If a temporary sign conflicts with a permanent one, the temporary sign is followed ⟦33⟧.
Markings and signs often duplicate each other: a crossing - signs 5.16.1-5.16.3 and (or) marking 1.14.1-1.14.3 ⟦34⟧; stop line 1.12 - sign 5.33 ⟦35⟧.
lesson.tip: In winter, when markings are covered with snow, look at the signs: they take priority.

list: Less than 3 m between the car and a solid line (other than the line marking the edge of the carriageway), if this obstructs traffic ⟦36⟧.
On a pedestrian crossing and within 5 m before it ⟦37⟧.
At a stopping area marked with marking 1.17, and within 15 m of it, except for category M2 and M3 vehicles ⟦38⟧.
Within 30 m of the edge of the intersecting carriageway, except on the side opposite a side approach of a T-junction with a solid line or a central reservation ⟦39⟧.
At yellow solid line 1.4 you cannot stop; at yellow broken line 1.10 you cannot leave the car parked.
lesson.tip: Stopping means up to 5 minutes, or longer if needed for boarding, alighting, loading or unloading. If you stay longer than 5 minutes for any other reason, that is parking.

keyFacts: You may cross 1.1 and 1.2 to stop on the shoulder, and 1.1 when driving around an obstruction if there is no other way round it ⟦2⟧
Lines 1.5-1.8 may be crossed from either side ⟦3⟧
1.11 is crossed from the side of the broken line; from the side of the solid line, only when completing overtaking or driving around an obstruction ⟦4⟧
1.3 separates oncoming flows on roads with 4 or more lanes; 1.5 on roads with 2 or 3 lanes ⟦5⟧
Yellow lines: 1.4 - no stopping, 1.10 - no parking, 1.17 - route vehicle stops and taxi ranks ⟦6⟧
1.12 is the stopping place at sign 2.5 or a prohibitory traffic light signal ⟦7⟧
Arrow 1.18 allowing a left turn from the far left lane also allows a U-turn ⟦8⟧
Stopping is prohibited on a crossing and within 5 m before it, and also if less than 3 m remains before a solid line and this obstructs traffic ⟦9⟧
The traffic controller's signals take priority over markings ⟦10⟧
If signs (including temporary ones) and marking lines conflict, or the markings are hard to see, the signs are followed ⟦11⟧
Route vehicles, other public transport including taxis, and category M3 vehicles use the lane marked with the letter “A” (1.23) ⟦12⟧
mistakes: Crossing the double solid line to turn into a yard. Line 1.3 must not be crossed; there are no exceptions for it.
Confusing 1.4 and 1.10: the yellow solid line prohibits stopping, while the yellow broken line prohibits only parking.
Not noticing the approach line 1.6 and starting to overtake just before a solid line. Long dashes are a signal to finish the manoeuvre.
Crossing 1.11 from the side of the solid line to start overtaking. From the side of the solid line, it may be crossed only when completing overtaking or driving around an obstruction.
Stopping on the stop line or beyond it. You must stop before line 1.12.
Thinking that markings take priority over signs. Where signs, including temporary ones, conflict with markings, the signs are followed ⟦13⟧.

questions.q: Oncoming traffic flows are separated by a double solid line. May you cross it to turn left into a yard?
options: No, crossing lines 1.1-1.3 is prohibited
Yes, if there is no oncoming traffic
Yes, if you signal with the indicator
Only during daylight hours
questions.explain: A double solid line is marking 1.3. Crossing lines 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3 is prohibited, and for 1.3 there are not even any exceptions.

questions.q: A broken-down truck is stopped in your lane. You can only drive around it by crossing a single solid line, and the oncoming lane is clear. What should you do?
options: Wait for a tow truck: a solid line must never be crossed
Drive around the truck on the right, along the shoulder, without crossing the solid line
Make a U-turn across the solid line and look for a way round on another road
Drive around it across the solid line: this is allowed when driving around an obstruction
questions.explain: Crossing 1.1 is allowed as an exception when driving around an obstruction, if there is no other way round it, and driving along the shoulder is not allowed ⟦40⟧. The obstruction is on your side, so give way to oncoming traffic ⟦41⟧. A double solid line 1.3 must not be crossed this way.

questions.q: Line 1.11 is marked to your left: on the side of your lane it is solid, on the other side it is broken. When may you cross it?
options: No, you must never cross this kind of solid line
Yes, at any time, in the same way as an ordinary broken line
Only when completing overtaking or driving around an obstruction
Only in order to make a U-turn or to drive into a yard
questions.explain: Line 1.11 may be crossed from the side of the broken line, and from the side of the solid line only when completing overtaking or driving around an obstruction.

questions.q: The broken centre line has changed: the dashes have become roughly three times longer than the gaps. What does this warn of?
options: An uncontrolled intersection is coming up soon
Solid line 1.1 or 1.11 will begin soon
An acceleration or deceleration lane will begin soon
A U-turn across the centre line is allowed here
questions.explain: This is the approach line 1.6. It warns that you are approaching marking 1.1 or 1.11, which separates traffic flows. It is too late to start overtaking.

questions.q: A yellow solid line is marked along the kerb. What does this mean?
options: Stopping is prohibited here
Only parking is prohibited here
This is a taxi rank
This is the edge of the carriageway on a motorway
questions.explain: Yellow solid line 1.4 marks places where stopping (and therefore parking too) is prohibited.

questions.q: A yellow broken line is marked along the edge of the carriageway. May you stop here briefly to let a passenger out?
options: No: this line prohibits both stopping and parking
Yes, but only with the hazard warning lights on
Yes: this line prohibits only parking
No: only taxis may stop at this line
questions.explain: Yellow broken line 1.10 marks places where parking is prohibited. You may stop here to let a passenger out, and hazard warning lights are not needed for this.

questions.q: What does a yellow zigzag line at the edge of the carriageway mark?
options: A parking place for vehicles of people with disabilities
A speed hump on the carriageway
A section where overtaking and U-turns are prohibited
A route vehicle stop or a taxi rank
questions.explain: Marking 1.17 marks route vehicle stops and taxi ranks.

questions.q: A route bus and a taxi are pulling up at a marked route vehicle stop. A yellow solid line 1.4 is marked along the edge here. Who is allowed to stop to board or set down passengers?
options: Only the bus driver
Only the taxi driver
Both drivers
Neither of them
questions.explain: Line 1.4 prohibits stopping, but it does not apply to route vehicles ⟦42⟧. A bus on its route stops at its own stop, but a taxi is not a route vehicle: it may not stop here ⟦43⟧.

questions.q: Marking 1.13 (a line of triangles) is marked across the lane before the entrance to an intersection. What does it mean?
options: A place where you must always stop, even if the road is clear
A place where you stop if necessary, giving way
A place where a speed hump is installed before the intersection
A place where a lane for route vehicles begins
questions.explain: Marking 1.13 shows the place where a driver, if necessary, stops, giving way to traffic on the intersecting road. If there is no one to give way to, you do not need to stop.

questions.q: You are driving in the far left lane. Before the intersection, a marking 1.18 “left” arrow is marked on it. May you make a U-turn from this lane?
options: No: the arrow allows only a left turn
Yes, but only on a green traffic light arrow
No: a U-turn is allowed only for route vehicles
Yes: such an arrow also allows a U-turn
questions.explain: As described for marking 1.18: an arrow that allows a left turn from the far left lane also allows a U-turn from that lane.

questions.q: The lane-control signals are switched off. Line 1.9 is marked to the left of your lane, and oncoming traffic is travelling beyond it. May you cross this line to overtake a slow truck?
options: Yes: line 1.9 may be crossed from either side
No: crossing this line 1.9 is prohibited
Yes, if no oncoming vehicles are in sight
Yes, but only to turn left
questions.explain: While the lane-control signals are switched off, line 1.9 separates oncoming traffic flows, and crossing it is prohibited. While the signals are off, line 1.9 may be crossed only if it is on the driver's right ⟦44⟧.

questions.q: The centre line is solid. Which paths may you continue along?
options: Only A
Only B
Both
None
questions.explain: Both paths cross solid line 1.1: turning into the yard and making a U-turn. Crossing lines 1.1-1.3 is prohibited; exceptions exist only for stopping on the shoulder and driving around an obstruction. You can reach the yard by making a U-turn where that is allowed.

questions.q: The centre line is broken. Which paths may you continue along?
options: Only A
Only B
Both
Neither
questions.explain: Broken line 1.5 may be crossed from either side. There are no signs here prohibiting a turn or a U-turn, so you may both turn into the yard and make a U-turn. In doing so, you must give way to oncoming vehicles ⟦45⟧.

questions.q: Oncoming traffic flows are separated by line 1.11; on the side of your lane it is broken. Which paths may you continue along?
options: Only A
Only B
Both
Neither
questions.explain: Line 1.11 may be crossed from the side of the broken line. The broken line is nearer to you, so you may both turn into the yard and make a U-turn, giving way to oncoming traffic ⟦46⟧. This is exactly why such a line is marked at places for U-turns and for entering and leaving.

questions.q: Oncoming traffic flows are separated by line 1.11; on the side of your lane it is solid. Which paths may you continue along?
options: Only A
Only B
Both
None
questions.explain: From the side of the solid line, line 1.11 may be crossed only when completing overtaking or driving around an obstruction. Turning into the yard and making a U-turn are not among these cases, so both paths are prohibited. Oncoming drivers, for whom the broken line is nearer, are allowed to make such manoeuvres.

questions.q: Both drivers want to turn left into a yard. Which of them does the marking allow to do this?
options: Only you
Only the driver of the blue car
Both
Neither
questions.explain: Line 1.11 is broken on the side of your lane and solid on the oncoming side. It may be crossed from the side of the broken line, so you may turn. The blue car would have to cross the line from the side of the solid line, and that is allowed only when completing overtaking or driving around an obstruction.

questions.q: The solid centre line is interrupted by a short stretch of line 1.11, broken on your side. Which paths may you continue along?
options: Only A
Only B
Both
Neither
questions.explain: Line 1.11 is marked where U-turns, entering and leaving are allowed. It may be crossed from the side of the broken line, so the U-turn along A is allowed. To enter the yard along B, you would have to cross solid line 1.1, and that is prohibited.

questions.q: The edge of the carriageway is marked with a solid line. May you cross it to stop on the shoulder?
options: Yes, but only during daylight hours
No: a solid line must not be crossed
Yes: line 1.1 may be crossed for this purpose
Yes, but only if the car has broken down
questions.explain: Lines 1.1 and 1.2 may be crossed to stop on the shoulder. Under the Rules, stopping is allowed primarily on the right-hand shoulder, and if there is none, at the edge of the carriageway ⟦47⟧.

questions.q: You get a flat tyre on an out-of-town motorway. The edge of the carriageway is marked with wide solid line 1.2, and there is a shoulder beyond it. What should you do?
options: Make a U-turn through a gap in the central reservation and drive unhurriedly to a service station
Stop on the central reservation, switch on the hazard warning lights and wait
Stop in your lane, since line 1.2 is not crossed, and switch on the hazard warning lights
Drive across line 1.2 onto the shoulder, switch on the hazard warning lights and put out the warning triangle
questions.explain: In the event of a forced stop on a motorway, the vehicle is moved to the right of the line marking the edge of the carriageway ⟦48⟧, and line 1.2 may be crossed to stop on the shoulder. Then switch on the hazard warning lights and put out the warning triangle not less than 30 m from the car ⟦49⟧. Making a U-turn and driving into service gaps in the central reservation on a motorway are prohibited ⟦50⟧.

questions.q: In a traffic jam, the driver of the blue car has crossed the solid line marking the edge of the carriageway and is driving along the shoulder. Is he breaking the rules?
options: No, not if he drives slowly and takes care not to obstruct pedestrians
Yes: driving along the shoulder is not allowed, even to get around a traffic jam
No: the solid line marking the edge of the road may always be crossed
Yes, but only if the shoulder is unpaved
questions.explain: The solid line at the edge is marking 1.1. It may be crossed to stop on the shoulder, but not to drive along it: driving on shoulders is not allowed ⟦51⟧.

questions.q: What does black-and-white vertical marking 2.3 mark?
options: The lower edge of the span of a bridge or flyover
Guide posts, tank obstacles and barrier supports
Round bollards on central reservations and islands
Kerbs on hazardous sections of road
questions.explain: Marking 2.3 is applied to round bollards installed on central reservations or traffic islands. The other options are also vertical markings: 2.2 is the lower edge of a span, 2.4 is guide posts and barrier supports, 2.7 is kerbs on hazardous sections. Bollards in the middle of the road are passed on the right, unless signs or markings require otherwise ⟦52⟧.

questions.q: A broken-down car is stopped in the left lane. Which path may you use to drive around it?
options: Only A
Only B
Both
Neither: you must wait for a tow truck
questions.explain: Crossing double solid line 1.3 is prohibited, and there is no exception for it to drive around an obstruction: that exception is made only for the single line 1.1. On a road with four lanes, driving onto the oncoming side is also prohibited ⟦53⟧. Drive around using the right-hand lane, giving way to those already travelling in it ⟦54⟧.

questions.q: The lanes in your direction are separated by a solid line. Which paths may you continue along?
options: Only A
Only B
Both
Neither
questions.explain: Solid line 1.1 marks not only the centre line but also lane boundaries in hazardous places. You must not change lanes across it. Continue in your own lane; you may change lanes where the line becomes broken.

questions.q: On which section of the centre line is the approach line 1.6 marked?
options: On section A
On section B
On section C
It is not in the diagram
questions.explain: The approach line 1.6 is broken, but its dashes are roughly 3 times longer than the gaps. Section A has an ordinary broken line 1.5, section B has the approach line, and section C has solid line 1.1. Once you see 1.6, you no longer start to overtake: a solid line is ahead.

questions.q: You have changed onto the deceleration lane to exit right, but realise this is not your exit. The deceleration lane is separated by wide broken line 1.8. May you return to the main lane?
options: No: you may only exit from the deceleration lane
Yes: vehicles on the main lane must let you in
Yes, giving way to vehicles on the main lane
No: line 1.8 may be crossed in one direction only
questions.explain: Lines 1.5-1.8 may be crossed from either side ⟦55⟧, so you may return from the deceleration lane. This is a lane change: give way to those travelling on the main lane without changing direction ⟦56⟧.

questions.q: Within the intersection, the lane boundaries continue as short dashes with equal gaps. What marking is this?
options: 1.6: approach to a solid marking line
1.7: lane boundaries within an intersection
1.8: the boundary of an acceleration or deceleration lane
1.9: the boundaries of lanes with reversible traffic
questions.explain: Line 1.7 shows which lane to continue in through the intersection. It is especially helpful when turning from several lanes. Like lines 1.5, 1.6 and 1.8, it may be crossed from either side.

questions.q: You are driving in town in the far right lane. The adjacent lane to the left is marked with lines 1.9 on both sides, and a green lane-control signal arrow pointing down is lit above it. May you change onto that lane?
options: No: line 1.9 may be crossed only when it is located to your right
No: you enter a reversible lane only in order to turn left or to make a U-turn
Yes: with the lane-control signal on, this line may be crossed from either side
Yes, but only in heavy traffic, when your own lane is occupied
questions.explain: A green arrow pointing down permits travel in the lane above which it is lit ⟦57⟧. When the lane-control signals are on, line 1.9, where it separates lanes running in the same direction, may be crossed from either side. The rule “only if the line is on your right” applies when there are no lane-control signals or they are switched off.

questions.q: You are driving in a lane marked with lines 1.9 on both sides. The lane-control signals have just switched off. What should you do?
options: Immediately change lane to the right, beyond line 1.9
Continue in this lane to the nearest intersection
Stop and wait for the signals to come back on
Change lane to the left, closer to the oncoming flow
questions.explain: When the lane-control signals switch off, the driver immediately changes lane to the right, beyond line 1.9. You must not stay in the reversible lane: oncoming traffic may start to use it, and entering such a lane while the signals are off is prohibited ⟦58⟧.

questions.q: There is no traffic on the main road. Are you required to stop at line 1.13?
options: No, but you must sound the horn before pulling out
Yes: you must always stop at line 1.13
No: you stop only if you need to give way
Yes, if the intersection is outside a built-up area
questions.explain: Marking 1.13 shows the place where a driver, if necessary, stops, giving way to traffic on the intersecting road. Sign 2.4 requires you to give way, not to stop, and if there is no one to give way to, you may drive on without stopping. Compare this with sign 2.5 and stop line 1.12: there, stopping is always mandatory.

questions.q: You are turning right. Where must you stop, if necessary, to let a truck pass?
options: Wherever is convenient: this line requires nothing
Before line 1.13
Beyond line 1.13, right at the edge of the main road
Right on line 1.13
questions.explain: Line 1.13, made of triangles, shows the place where a driver, if necessary, stops, giving way to traffic on the intersecting road. The truck is on the main road, and sign 2.4 requires you to give way to it, so wait before the line.

questions.q: A triangle is marked on the lane before the intersection, as shown in the diagram. What does it warn of?
options: That you are approaching line 1.13, where you give way
That you are approaching the start of a main road
That you are approaching a speed hump
That you are approaching an uncontrolled pedestrian crossing
questions.explain: This is marking 1.20. It warns that you are approaching line 1.13, where you stop if necessary, giving way to traffic on the intersecting road. Sign 2.4 is usually placed nearby.

questions.q: The word “STOP” is written on your lane. What does this mean?
options: Stopping and parking are prohibited here, at the inscription
There is a dead end ahead and no way through
You must stop right at this inscription, not further on
There is a stop line ahead, where you will need to stop
questions.explain: The word “STOP” is marking 1.21. It warns that you are approaching stop line 1.12, which is used together with sign 2.5. You stop not at the inscription, but before the stop line.

questions.q: The red signal is on. Which driver has stopped correctly?
options: Only the driver of the blue car
Only the driver of the white car
Both
Neither
questions.explain: At a prohibitory traffic light signal, you stop before stop line 1.12 ⟦59⟧. The white car is stopped before it, while the blue car has driven onto the line with its front end. Even if there is still room before the crossing, you must stop before the stop line.

questions.q: The traffic controller has raised an arm straight up. Where must you stop?
options: Nowhere: if the intersection is empty, you may drive through
Before the stop line
Next to the traffic controller
Right after the stop line, at the edge of the intersecting road
questions.explain: An arm raised straight up prohibits movement. At a prohibitory traffic light or traffic controller signal, drivers stop before stop line 1.12 (or sign 5.33), and if there is none, before the intersecting carriageway ⟦60⟧.

questions.q: There is a “zebra crossing” ahead of you, with no “Pedestrian crossing” signs. A pedestrian is already crossing on it. What should you do?
options: Give way: the “zebra crossing” alone is enough to mark a crossing
Drive on: without “Pedestrian crossing” signs, this is not a crossing
Give way only if the pedestrian raises a hand
Sound the horn at the pedestrian and go first
questions.explain: A pedestrian crossing is marked with signs 5.16.1-5.16.3 and (or) marking 1.14.1-1.14.3 ⟦61⟧. So a “zebra crossing” on its own is enough. At an uncontrolled crossing, the driver gives way to pedestrians ⟦62⟧.

questions.q: Arrows (marking 1.14.2) are marked on the “zebra crossing”, as shown in the diagram. What do they show?
options: The direction for vehicles to drive around the crossing
That traffic on the crossing is controlled by traffic lights
A place where vehicles may make a U-turn
The direction pedestrians walk across the crossing
questions.explain: Markings 1.14.1 and 1.14.2 mark an uncontrolled pedestrian crossing, and the arrows of 1.14.2 show the direction pedestrians should walk across it. For the driver, the rules are the same as for any “zebra crossing”: give way to pedestrians ⟦63⟧.

questions.q: How does a pedestrian crossing marked with 1.14.3 differ from one marked with 1.14.1?
options: Marking 1.14.3 marks an underground pedestrian crossing
It does not: this is exactly the same marking
At a 1.14.3 crossing, traffic is controlled by traffic lights
Marking 1.14.3 marks a cycle track crossing
questions.explain: 1.14.1 and 1.14.2 mark an uncontrolled crossing, while 1.14.3 marks a crossing where traffic is controlled by traffic lights. There, the driver follows the traffic light signal, but on a permissive signal still gives way to pedestrians who are finishing crossing ⟦64⟧.

questions.q: Which driver is allowed to stop?
options: Only the blue car
Only the green car
Both
Neither
questions.explain: Stopping is prohibited on pedestrian crossings and within 5 m before them ⟦65⟧. The green car is stopped only 3 m before the “zebra crossing” and blocks pedestrians from other drivers' view. The blue car has stopped after the crossing, where there is no such restriction.

questions.q: Where a cycle track crosses the carriageway, a marking made of squares is applied, as shown in the diagram. What is its number?
questions.explain: Marking 1.15 marks the place where a cycle track crosses the carriageway. Outside an intersection, at such an uncontrolled crossing, the cyclist gives way to vehicles on the road ⟦66⟧, but the driver still needs to be ready to brake.

questions.q: A traffic island is marked in the middle of the road. Which paths may you continue along?
options: Only A
Only B
Both
Neither
questions.explain: Marking 1.16.1 marks a traffic island where oncoming flows are divided. Islands and other objects in the middle of the carriageway are passed on the right, unless signs or markings require otherwise ⟦67⟧. Path B leads onto the oncoming side, across solid lines and over the island.

questions.q: The island in the diagram divides oncoming traffic flows. Which marking 1.16 applies here?
options: 1.16.1 - dividing oncoming flows
1.16.2 - dividing flows in one direction
1.16.3 - merging flows
This is not 1.16, but a parking place marking
questions.explain: Marking 1.16 marks traffic islands: 1.16.1 where oncoming flows are divided, 1.16.2 where flows in one direction are divided, 1.16.3 where flows merge. Here the island stands between the oncoming lanes, so this is 1.16.1.

questions.q: Which driver is allowed to stop?
options: The bus and the green car
Only the bus
All three
The bus and the blue car
questions.explain: Marking 1.17 marks a route vehicle stop. Stopping at the stopping area and within 15 m of it is prohibited for everyone except category M2 and M3 vehicles, which include the bus ⟦68⟧. The green car is stopped 10 m before the stop and is breaking the rule; the blue car is 20 m after it.

questions.q: You are in the left lane and have already passed the marking arrows. Which paths may you continue along?
options: Only A
Only B
Both
Neither
questions.explain: Arrows 1.18 show where you may drive from each lane. Only the “ahead” arrow is marked in your lane, so turning left from it is prohibited, even though the lane is the far left one and the intersection is clear.

questions.q: You are in the right lane and have already passed the marking arrows. Which paths may you continue along?
options: Only A
Only B
Both
Neither
questions.explain: Arrow 1.18 in your lane allows only a right turn. You may not drive straight ahead from this lane; for that you would have needed to move into the left lane in good time.

questions.q: You are in the left lane and have already passed the marking arrows. Which paths may you continue along?
options: Only A and B
Only B
All three
Only B and C
questions.explain: The arrow in your lane allows ahead and left. Marking 1.18, where it allows a left turn from the far left lane, also allows a U-turn from it. So you may take any of the three paths.

questions.q: Arrow 1.18 with a dead-end symbol is marked on the lane: its branch to the right ends at a short transverse bar. What does it mean?
options: A right turn is allowed only for route vehicles
You must stop before turning
Turning into the nearest carriageway is prohibited
There is a dead end ahead, with no way through
questions.explain: Marking 1.18 with a dead-end symbol is applied to show that turning into the nearest carriageway is prohibited. It does not close off driving straight ahead.

questions.q: Road works have closed your lane. Sign 4.2.2 “Keep left” shows the way around, but the centre line is solid. What should you do?
options: Wait for the works to finish: a solid line must not be crossed
Drive around the works on the right, along the shoulder, without crossing the solid line
Make a U-turn across the solid line and look for another road
Drive around on the left, as the sign requires: it takes priority over the marking
questions.explain: If the meanings of signs, including temporary ones, and marking lines conflict with each other, drivers are guided by the signs. Moreover, single solid line 1.1 may be crossed when driving around an obstruction, if there is no other way round it. The obstruction is on your side, so let oncoming traffic pass ⟦69⟧.
questions.ref: Annex 2 (signs take priority over markings), marking 1.1; Annex 1, sign 4.2.2; para. 83

questions.q: The lane arrows are covered with snow and cannot be seen. Sign 5.8.1 on the right shows: from the left lane, left only; from the middle lane, ahead; from the right lane, ahead and right. You are in the left lane. Which paths may you continue along?
options: Only A
Only B
Both
Neither
questions.explain: If the markings are not clearly visible or conflict with the signs, you are guided by the signs. Sign 5.8.1 allows only a left turn from the left lane, so you may not drive straight ahead from it.
questions.ref: Annex 2 (signs take priority over markings); Annex 1, sign 5.8.1

questions.q: Which driver is allowed to stop?
options: Only the green car
Only the blue car
Both
Neither
questions.explain: Yellow solid line 1.4 prohibits stopping, but only where it is marked. The green car is stopped at this line and is breaking the rule. The blue car has stopped after it ends, where stopping is allowed.

questions.q: Which driver is allowed to park?
options: Only the green car
Both
Only the blue car
Neither
questions.explain: Yellow broken line 1.10 prohibits parking, but only where it is marked. The green car may only stop here: to let a passenger out or wait up to 5 minutes. The blue car is stopped after the line ends, where parking is allowed.

questions.q: A yellow broken line is marked along the edge. A taxi is waiting for a passenger with the meter running. Who is allowed to park?
options: Only the blue car
Only the taxi
Both
Neither
questions.explain: Line 1.10 prohibits parking, but it does not apply, in particular, to taxis with the meter running or to vehicles driven by people with group I or II disability. The blue car may only stop here.

questions.q: You stopped at a yellow broken line and went into a shop for 20 minutes. Did you break the rules?
options: No, if you leave your phone number behind the windscreen
Yes: this is already parking, and line 1.10 prohibits it
No: line 1.10 prohibits only stopping
No, if you switch on the hazard warning lights
questions.explain: Stopping means ceasing movement for up to 5 minutes, or longer if needed for boarding, alighting, loading or unloading. Going off on your own business for 20 minutes is parking, and yellow broken line 1.10 prohibits exactly that: parking.

questions.q: A yellow solid line is marked not on the asphalt, but along the top of the kerb. May you stop at this edge?
options: Yes: the marking applies only on the carriageway
Yes, but only for no longer than 5 minutes
No: on the kerb too, this line prohibits stopping
Yes, if you switch on the hazard warning lights
questions.explain: Marking 1.4 marks places where stopping is prohibited. It is applied at the edge of the carriageway or along the top of the kerb, and used on its own or together with sign 3.27. The meaning is the same in both cases.

questions.q: What does the inscription “M-36” on the carriageway mean?
options: A permitted speed of 36 km/h
The number of the traffic lane
The distance to a built-up area in kilometres
The road (route) number
questions.explain: This is marking 1.22; it shows the road (route) number. It does not impose any restrictions, but helps you stay on the right route, especially at forks.

questions.q: The letter “A” is marked on the right-hand lane. Who is allowed to drive in this lane?
options: The bus, the taxi and the truck
Everyone, if the lane is clear
The bus and the taxi
Only the bus
questions.explain: The letter “A” is marking 1.23: a lane for route vehicles, other public transport and other category M3 vehicles. Under the Rules, a taxi counts as public transport. A truck may not drive or stop in this lane ⟦70⟧.

questions.q: Yellow marking 1.28, in the form of a grid, is marked on the intersection. The light is green for you, but there is a traffic jam right beyond the intersection. What should you do?
options: Do not enter the intersection until there is room beyond it
Drive around the jam using the oncoming lane
Enter and wait in the middle of the intersection, since the light is green for you
Enter if the light for the intersecting road is currently red
questions.explain: Marking 1.28 marks the controlled area of an intersection. Entering the intersection is prohibited if there is a jam beyond it and you would have to stop there, obstructing crossing traffic ⟦71⟧. When the signal changes, a car stuck there would block the path of those driving across.

questions.q: The street is narrow: a car parked at the edge can be driven around only by crossing the centre line. Which driver is allowed to stop?
options: Only the green car
Only the blue car
Both
Neither
questions.explain: Stopping is prohibited if less than 3 m remains between the car and a solid marking line (other than the line marking the edge of the carriageway) and this obstructs traffic ⟦72⟧. The green car can only be driven around by crossing a solid line, which is prohibited. The blue car is driven around by crossing a broken line, so it may stop there.

questions.q: Arrows are marked on your lane, as shown in the diagram, and a “Road narrows on the right” sign stands on the right. What should you do?
options: Stop and wait until the left lane is completely clear
Drive around the narrowing along the shoulder
Change lane to the left in good time, giving way to the white car
Drive to the end of the lane and change lane there, ahead of the white car
questions.explain: These are arrows 1.19: they warn that you are approaching a narrowing of the carriageway, and your lane will soon end. Change lane in good time and give way to those already travelling in the left lane in the same direction ⟦73⟧. Driving around along the shoulder is not allowed ⟦74⟧.

questions.q: You are exiting a yard. The centre line is 1.11; on the side of the lane nearer to you it is broken. Which paths may you continue along?
options: Only A
Only B
Both
Neither
questions.explain: When exiting to the left, you cross line 1.11 from the side of the broken line, and that is allowed. Turning right is allowed in any case. When exiting the yard, give way to everyone travelling on the road ⟦75⟧.

questions.q: You are exiting a yard. The centre line is 1.11; on the side of the lane nearer to you it is solid. Which paths may you continue along?
options: Only A
Only B
Both
Neither
questions.explain: To go left, you would have to cross line 1.11 from the side of the solid line. That is allowed only when completing overtaking or driving around an obstruction, so going left is not allowed. You may exit to the right, giving way to those travelling on the road ⟦76⟧.

questions.q: The double solid line breaks opposite a road joining from the left. May you turn left here?
options: No: you may not turn left on a road with a double solid line
Only if there is sign 5.8.1 with a left-turn arrow
No: turning left is allowed only at controlled intersections
Yes: at the gap you do not need to cross the line
questions.explain: The prohibition concerns crossing line 1.3 itself. At the junction, the line is interrupted, so a left turn is allowed unless signs prohibit it. Priority is determined by the rules for passing through intersections: you will usually have to let oncoming traffic going straight ahead pass first.

questions.q: What is the number of the solid line that marks the edge of the carriageway on an ordinary out-of-town road?
questions.explain: The edge of the carriageway on ordinary roads is marked with line 1.1. Wide solid line 1.2 marks the edge of the carriageway only on motorways. Both may be crossed to stop on the shoulder.

questions.q: The centre line is solid before the intersection. May you turn left at the intersection?
options: Only on a green filter arrow
No: the solid line prohibits a left turn
Only if a 1.18 “left” arrow is marked on the lane
Yes: there is no solid line on the intersection itself
questions.explain: The marking prohibits crossing the line itself. At the intersection, the solid line is interrupted, and the left turn is made without crossing it. Signs or arrows 1.18 could prohibit the turn, but there are none here.

questions.q: You need to turn left, but you are in the right lane, and the lanes are separated by a solid line. What should you do?
options: Drive straight ahead or turn right, and make a U-turn where it is allowed
Change into the left lane across the solid line and turn
Turn left straight from the right lane, letting vehicles on the left pass first
Stop and wait for drivers in the left lane to let you in
questions.explain: Solid line 1.1 between the lanes prohibits changing lanes, and arrow 1.18 in your lane allows only ahead and right. Turning left from the right lane is not allowed either. Drive as the arrow allows, and make a U-turn or turn where it is possible.

questions.q: You are a taxi driver. The passenger asks to be set down right at a bus stop, at the yellow zigzag line. May you stop here?
options: Yes: under the Rules a taxi counts as public transport
Yes, if there is no bus standing at the stop right now
Yes, but only for a time of no longer than one minute
No: this place is only for category M2 and M3 vehicles
questions.explain: Marking 1.17 marks a route vehicle stop. Stopping at the stopping area and within 15 m of it is prohibited for everyone except category M2 and M3 vehicles ⟦77⟧. A passenger-car taxi is not among them, even though it may drive in the lane for route vehicles.

questions.q: Alternating black and white stripes are marked on bridge piers, barriers at hazardous bends and kerbs. What is this?
options: Vertical markings: they show the outline of structures
Temporary markings applied for the duration of repairs
A warning that a permanent police checkpoint is ahead
Markings that prohibit parking near these structures
questions.explain: Vertical markings 2.1-2.7 are a combination of black and white stripes on road structures and road equipment. For example, 2.1 is applied to hazardous elements of bridges and flyovers, 2.5 to barriers on small-radius bends and steep descents, and 2.7 to kerbs on hazardous sections.
